document_title: UT San Antonio's flood sensor runs its AI on the device
_note: Slide strings read off the render report's text nodes and each frame's own source line by build_copy.py.
caption:
A low-water crossing in San Antonio.

UT San Antonio's September 28th release says flood risk there often climbs block by block before regional alerts sound.

Chen Pan's team built a prototype that judges that risk on the device itself. Four optical water-level sensors at varying heights sit on one solar powered node. TinyML on its microcontroller judges imminent flood risk with no central server. Parts for one prototype run roughly $150 to $220.

A real flood would be the test. The release reports 98.82% validation accuracy in initial assessments after training. It names no site, no city or county running it and no false alarm or missed event figure. The team aims the design at small coastal towns.

The release holds a validation score and a parts cost. Where is the record of the node in a real flood?

#SanAntonio #UTSA #TinyML

S1.headline: It judges flood risk on the device
S1.body: UT San Antonio's prototype runs its AI on the device, with no server. Its release says risk at San Antonio's low-water crossings often climbs before regional alerts sound. Drawn to illustrate.

S2.kicker: UT San Antonio and UT Arlington
S2.headline: Radar can read the storm low
S2.body: UT San Antonio's release says regional models can miss very local flash floods. UT Arlington checked radar against more than 300 rain gauges and found it can read storm totals roughly 20% low under some conditions.

S3.headline: Four water sensors stacked on one node
S3.body: Four optical water-level sensors at varying heights, plus temperature, humidity, light and precipitation. Drawn to illustrate.
strings: Four water sensors stacked on one node
Four optical water-level sensors at varying heights, plus temperature, humidity, light and precipitation. Drawn to illustrate.

S4.headline: No server in the loop
S4.body: TinyML shrinks a machine learning model to run on a small, low-power microcontroller. The model on the node judges imminent flood risk from current and recent readings without a central server.
strings: TinyML shrinks a machine learning model to run on a small, low-power microcontroller. The model on the node judges imminent flood risk from current and recent readings without a central server.

S5.headline: Over a half-mile in town, up to five miles open
S5.body: The node's LoRa radio reaches more than a half-mile through city streets and up to five miles in open areas, the release says. No site is named, so the circles show scale only.
strings: Over a half-mile in town, up to five miles open

S6.headline: $150 to $220 in parts
S6.body: Parts for one prototype station cost roughly $150 to $220, the release says. A Texas Coastal Management Program grant approved by the Texas Land Commissioner helped fund the work. The parts are drawn to illustrate.

S8.headline: No flood test is named
S8.body: The release names no installation site, no city or county running it and no field test against a real flood. It gives no false alarm or missed event figure. It describes a prototype the team aims at small coastal towns. Drawn to illustrate.

S9.headline: Turn around at the water
S9.body: The National Weather Service cites the CDC. Over half of flood drownings happen when a vehicle is driven into flood water. Whatever a sensor reports, the turn is the driver's. Drawn to illustrate.
